questions.question_text: A manager conducts an in-person, face-to-face performance appraisal survey asking employees: 'Do you feel our management team is effective?' Why might the responses be inaccurate?

options.text: Employees may alter their answers to please the interviewer or avoid a negative appraisal
The sample size is mathematically unrepresentative
options.why: The question addresses administration bias, not numerical sample size.

options.text: The survey lacks a group receiving a comparison treatment
options.why: This is a survey of opinions, not an experiment comparing treatments. The stated risk is pressure during the interview.

options.text: Employees have severe long-term recall memory errors
options.why: Rating current management does not require long-term retrospective memory recall.

questions.solution_text:
Employees may give flattering answers rather than honest criticism when management interviews them directly.
Employees may alter their answers to please the interviewer or avoid a negative appraisal.

questions.question_text:
A biology student investigates the effect of music on plant growth by playing rock music to $10$ potted plants on a sunny windowsill, but has no plants grown without music.
What is the fundamental flaw in this experiment?

options.text: There is no control group grown in silence under identical lighting and temperature
The music volume was recorded using an uncalibrated sound meter
options.why: The stem does not describe a sound meter or a calibration fault. It does explicitly lack a comparison group without music.

options.text: The plants were aware they were participating in an experiment
options.why: No change caused by participants noticing an observer is described. The stated design fault is the missing no-music group.

options.text: The survey questions were leading and double-barrelled
options.why: This is a plant biology experiment, not a questionnaire.

questions.solution_text:
Without a control group kept in quiet conditions, there is no way to know whether the plants grew because of sunlight, water, or the music.
There is no control group grown in silence under identical lighting and temperature.

questions.question_text:
A sleep clinic asks patients on 1 December to record the exact minute they fell asleep on each night of the preceding July.
Which data collection error will severely affect this data?

options.text: Recall error in self-reported retrospective logs
The observer effect from being watched while sleeping
options.why: The question asks patients to remember nights months earlier, rather than describing a direct observation that changes their behaviour.

options.text: Lack of a comparison group receiving a different treatment
options.why: This task collects remembered sleep times; it does not compare the effect of treatments.

options.text: Measurement error from a miscalibrated sleep-tracking device
options.why: No electronic tracking device is used; patients are self-reporting estimates from memory.

questions.solution_text:
Patients may not accurately recall exact sleep times from July when asked in December, leading to unreliable guesses.
Recall error in self-reported retrospective logs.

questions.question_text:
A gym trainer wants to evaluate whether a new pre-workout shake improves bench press strength.
The trainer tests $20$ athletes before taking the shake, gives them the shake, and tests them again $30$ minutes later.
How should the trainer improve this experiment to isolate the true effect of the shake?

options.text: Include a comparable control group given a shake without the new ingredient, under the same test conditions
Interview each athlete face-to-face with the gym owner present
options.why: Interviews with gym owners introduce interviewer bias rather than fixing experimental controls.

options.text: Ask athletes to recall their high school bench press records from memory
options.why: Using distant memory recall introduces recall error and reduces measurement accuracy.

options.text: Test the athletes only after running a marathon
options.why: Fatiguing athletes with a marathon would introduce severe confounding variables.

questions.solution_text:
A second test may differ because of warming up, practice or expectations rather than the new ingredient. A comparable control group helps check changes that would occur without that ingredient.
Include a comparable control group given a shake without the new ingredient, under the same test conditions.

questions.question_text:
A psychologist studies pedestrian walking speeds by standing openly on a footpath with a large video camera pointed directly at oncoming walkers.
What potential collection fault should be considered?

options.text: Observer effect: pedestrians may change their natural pace when they notice the camera
Recall error from pedestrians misremembering their speeds
options.why: Pedestrians are being recorded in real-time, not recalling past speeds from memory.

options.text: Lack of a control group receiving a different treatment
options.why: The study observes walking speeds; it does not compare experimental treatments.

options.text: Data transcription error during electronic scanning
options.why: The fault occurs at the observation stage due to visible camera presence.

questions.solution_text:
A visible camera may make pedestrians self-conscious and change how they normally walk.
Observer effect: pedestrians may change their natural pace when they notice the camera.

questions.question_text:
An experiment testing fuel efficiency runs Car A on flat highways at $80\text{ km/h}$ on a cool morning and Car B through congested city traffic at $40^{\circ}\text{C}$.
Which critical fault invalidates the comparison?

options.text: Confounding variables: driving terrain, speed, and ambient temperature differed between the two tests
The cars were not selected using stratified random sampling
options.why: The flaw is the uncontrolled experimental test conditions, not the car sample selection.

options.text: The fuel volume was measured with an anonymous survey
options.why: Fuel volume is a physical measurement, not a survey.

options.text: Drivers suffered from social desirability bias
options.why: The failure is in road and temperature conditions, not driver psychological social desirability.

questions.solution_text:
Because route, driving conditions, and temperature were not held constant, any difference in fuel use cannot be attributed to the cars.
Confounding variables: driving terrain, speed, and ambient temperature differed between the two tests.

questions.question_text:
A government agency mails $2000$ detailed forms asking citizens about their private financial debts.
Only $50$ completed forms are returned ($2.5\%$ response rate), and the agency publishes the findings without contacting non-respondents.
What data collection fault has occurred?

options.text: A risk of non-response bias because very few selected citizens replied and no follow-up was attempted
Observer effect caused by visible camera surveillance
options.why: Mail surveys involve no camera surveillance or visible observer effect.

options.text: Instrument measurement error from faulty electronic timing gates
options.why: Electronic timing gates relate to physical sports measurements, not mail surveys.

options.text: Failure to provide a placebo control group
options.why: Surveys do not use medical placebo control groups.

questions.solution_text:
$50\div2000\times100\%=2.5\%$ replied, so $97.5\%$ did not.
The respondents' debt levels may differ from those of non-respondents. Few replies and no follow-up leave this risk unchecked; the low rate alone does not prove which way the result is biased.
A risk of non-response bias because very few selected citizens replied and no follow-up was attempted.

questions.question_text:
An environmental research team tests water quality in a river.
The team measures water pH using an uncalibrated chemical probe that consistently reads $1.2$ units too acidic, and records temperatures using three different thermometers that disagree by up to $4^{\circ}\text{C}$.
How should the team fix their data collection procedure?

options.text: Check and calibrate the probe using known pH values, and use consistent calibrated thermometers
Ask local residents to guess the water pH based on memory
options.why: Residents' guesses do not check or correct the faulty instruments.

options.text: Replace the river water with a double-blind placebo liquid
options.why: Environmental river testing requires measuring the actual river, not placebo liquids.

options.text: Conduct face-to-face interviews with the fish in the river
options.why: This is nonsensical; environmental testing requires calibrated physical instruments.

questions.solution_text:
Check the probe against known pH values and adjust it to remove its consistent error. Check the thermometers against known temperatures and use a consistent measurement procedure.
Check and calibrate the probe using known pH values, and use consistent calibrated thermometers.
